x: In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Commentary on Sūrat ʿAmma Yatasāʾalūn (‘About What Are They Asking?’).
The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘About what do they ask one another?
n
About the tremendous news
n

, concerning which they differ (3). No indeed! They will come to know (4); again, no indeed! They will come to know (5).’ God says: Muḥammad, what are these Quraysh polytheists asking one another about? It is reported that they were disputing and arguing about what the Messenger of God called them to: acknowledging his prophethood, affirming what he brought from God, and believing in resurrection. God therefore asked His Prophet what they were discussing and disputing. Here fī (‘about’) and ʿan (‘concerning’) have the same meaning. Al-Ḥasan said that when the Prophet was sent, they began asking one another, and God revealed this verse, meaning the tremendous report. Abū Jaʿfar then says God explains what they ask about: the tremendous news.
The interpreters differed over what the tremendous news is. Mujāhid said it is the Qur’an.

Others said it is resurrection. Qatādah explained it as resurrection after death. Ibn Zayd said it is the Day of Resurrection: they said, ‘Is this the Day you claim we and our fathers will be brought back to life?’ They differed over it and did not believe it. God says, ‘Say: It is tremendous news, yet you turn away from it’ (Q 38:67–68). Some grammarians said Quraysh were speaking about the Qur’an … … and the question then means, ‘About what are they asking one another concerning the Qur’an?’ God says, ‘concerning which they differ,’ some affirming it and others denying it. That is their disagreement.

His saying, ‘concerning which they differ’: they have divided into two groups, one affirming it and the other denying it. Their mutual questioning is about this news. Qatādah said the matter is resurrection after death: people have split into believers and deniers. They all acknowledge death because they have witnessed it, but differ about resurrection after death. Another report from him gives the same explanation.

His saying, ‘No indeed!’: the matter is not as these polytheists claim … … who deny that God will raise them to life after their death. God threatens them for saying this: ‘They will come to know’ means that the disbelievers who deny God’s threat against His enemies will learn what He will do to them on the Day of Resurrection. He reinforces the warning by repeating it: matters are not as they claim, that God will not revive them after death or punish them for disbelief. When they meet God and face the evil deeds they sent ahead, they will know that the truth is otherwise. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk explained the first ‘they will know’ as referring to the disbelievers and the second as referring to the believers; he is also reported to have recited it that way.

x: The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Did We not make the earth a resting place (6), the mountains as stakes (7), create you in pairs (8), make your sleep a repose (9), make the night a covering (10), and make the day for livelihood (11)?’ God reminds these polytheists of His blessings, favors, and beneficence toward them, despite their ingratitude, and warns them of the kinds of punishment He has prepared when they return to Him. He says: Did We not make the earth for you as a resting place, so that you may settle and spread out upon it? Qatādah said it is like a carpet. ‘And the mountains as stakes’: God placed mountains as stakes in the earth so it would not sway with you. ‘We created you in pairs’ means males and females, tall and short, or ugly and handsome. ‘Their counterparts’ in ‘those who did wrong and their counterparts’ (Q 37:22) means their likes. ‘We made your sleep a repose’: We made your sleep rest and ease, in which you become still, as though dead and unaware, while remaining alive and your souls not having departed.

Sabt and subāt mean stillness; Saturday is called sabt because it is a day of rest and leisure. ‘We made the night a covering’: its darkness envelops and covers you like a garment, so you may rest from the activities you carried out by day. A poet says, ‘When they had put on the night, or when it had set …’ meaning they entered its darkness and were concealed by it. Qatādah said night is stillness.

His saying, ‘We made the day for livelihood’: We made the day bright for you so you may spread out … … to seek your livelihoods, conduct your worldly affairs, and seek God’s bounty. God called the day a livelihood because it enables His servants to go about seeking sustenance. A poet similarly attributes the act of not sleeping to the pillow when he means the person resting on it. Mujāhid said people seek God’s bounty during the day.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘We built above you seven mighty heavens (12), placed a blazing lamp (13), and sent down abundant water from the rain clouds (14).’ ‘We built above you’ means We roofed you over. God calls the roof a structure because Arabs call the roofs of houses—their heavens—buildings; the sky is a roof over the earth. He addresses them in their own language, since the revelation came in their language. ‘Seven mighty’ means firmly constructed, with no cracks or flaws, not worn down by the passage of nights and days.
His saying, ‘We placed a blazing lamp’: the lamp means the sun.
‘Blazing’ means burning brightly and illuminating.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the blazing lamp as illuminating and bright. Mujāhid said it shines and glitters. Qatādah said ‘blazing’ means luminous. Sufyān said its light sparkles.
His saying, ‘We sent down from the muʿṣirāt’: the interpreters differed over what is meant by muʿṣirāt.

Some said it means winds that squeeze as they blow. Ibn ʿAbbās said the muʿṣirāt are winds. ʿIkrimah is reported to have read ‘We sent down by the winds,’ meaning winds. Mujāhid likewise said winds; another report from him gives the same view. Qatādah said that in one reading it is ‘We sent down by the winds.’ Ibn Zayd also said winds and cited ‘God is the One who sends the winds, which then raise clouds’ (Q 30:48).

Others said muʿṣirāt are clouds that are laden with rain but have not yet rained, like a woman whose time for menstruation has approached but has not begun. Sufyān said muʿṣirāt are clouds. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Rabīʿ likewise said clouds.

Others said they are the heavens. Al-Ḥasan said ‘from the sky’; Qatādah and another report from him gave the same explanation. The soundest view is that God says He sent down water from the muʿṣirāt—clouds that have become full of water. This is preferable because of the three interpretations mentioned: winds contain no water to descend from them; water descends by means of winds. If the reading were ‘by the muʿṣirāt,’ winds could be intended. But the reading is ‘from the muʿṣirāt,’ showing that the clouds are meant. Even if bāʾ can sometimes follow in a meaning like min, the usual meaning of min is different and interpretation should follow the usual sense. The sky could also be intended, but rain most commonly descends from clouds. ‘Abundant water’ means water pouring down, following one flow after another, like the streaming of blood from sacrificial camels. Ibn ʿAbbās said it pours down; Mujāhid said the same; Qatādah said abundant water pours down; al-Rabīʿ said it is poured forth; and Sufyān said it comes in succession.

Others said thajjāj means plentiful. Ibn Zayd said it means plentiful. But the Arabs do not use thajj as an adjective for abundance; it means pouring continuously. The Prophet said, ‘The best pilgrimage is loud invocation and the pouring of sacrificial blood,’ using thajj for the spilling of blood from sacrificial camels … … One says thajajtu damahu, ‘I poured his blood’; the blood has been poured, and it flows forth.

x: The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘So that We may bring forth grain and plants (15), and gardens densely interwoven (16). The Day of Decision has an appointed time (17): the Day the Trumpet is blown and you come in multitudes (18), the heaven is opened and becomes gates (19), and the mountains are set moving and become a mirage (20).’ God says that by the water sent down from the rain clouds He brings forth grain. Grain is what the husks of cultivated plants contain and what is harvested; it is the plural of ḥabbah, just as shaʿīr (barley) is a collective of shaʿīrah and tamr (dates) a collective of tamrah. Vegetation is pasture grasses and crops that are grazed.
His saying, ‘and gardens densely interwoven’: We bring forth gardens—orchards—by that rain. ‘Gardens’ means the fruit of gardens; the word ‘fruit’ is omitted because the context makes it understood.

His saying, ‘densely interwoven’ means entwined and crowded together. Ibn ʿAbbās explained them as gathered together. Ibn ʿAbbās said the gardens are interwoven with one another. Mujāhid said they are dense. Qatādah said one part is joined to another. Sufyān likewise said they are dense. Ibn Zayd described them as interwoven one over another. Arab grammarians differed about the singular of alfāf: some Basrans said it is liff; some Kufans said liff or lafīf.

Others said alfāf may be a plural whose singular is itself collective, as in jannah laffāʾ, ‘a densely interwoven garden,’ and jinān lifāʾ. Some grammarians said they had not heard a tree called laffah; its singular is laffāʾ, its plural liff, and the plural of liff is alfāf, a plural of a plural. The correct view is that alfāf is the plural of liff or lafīf, since the interpreters agree it means interwoven. Laffāʾ means thick, and interweaving itself is not thickness unless one means thickness from the intertwining; then that would be a possible sense.

His saying, ‘The Day of Decision has an appointed time’: the Day when God judges between His creatures, giving each person his due from another, is an appointed time for what God has decreed for these deniers of resurrection and those like them. Qatādah said it is a Day God has magnified, when He judges between earlier and later peoples according to their deeds.

His saying, ‘the Day the Trumpet is blown’: the phrase ‘the Day the Trumpet is blown’ explains the Day of Decision, as though it said: the Day of Decision is the appointed time promised to these people, the Day the Trumpet is blown. The meaning of the Trumpet and the interpreters’ differences over it were explained earlier, so there is no need to repeat them here. The Trumpet is a horn into which the angel will blow. The Prophet said, ‘The Trumpet is a horn.’ Qatādah said al-ṣūr here means creation.
His saying, ‘and you come in multitudes’: you will come group after group and company after company.

The interpreters said similarly. Mujāhid explained it as groups. Each community to which God sent a messenger will come with the messenger sent to it, as in ‘the Day We call every people with their leader’ (Q 17:71).

His saying, ‘the heaven is opened and becomes gates’: the heaven will be split and cleft, becoming paths, though before that it was firm, without fissures or cracks. It is also said that it will be opened and become pieces like the boards cut to make doors for houses and dwellings. The meaning is ‘the heaven was opened and became pieces …’ … like doors. The comparison particle kāf was omitted, leaving ‘doors’ as the predicate. This is like saying in Arabic, ‘ʿAbd Allāh was a lion,’ meaning ‘like a lion.’

His saying, ‘the mountains are set moving and become a mirage’: the mountains will be scattered and uprooted, becoming dispersed dust to the viewer’s eye, like a mirage that someone far away thinks is water though it is actually dust.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Hell lies in ambush (21), a destination for the transgressors (22), where they will remain for ages (23). They will taste neither coolness nor drink (24), except scalding water and pus (25).’ God means that Hell is an ambush for those who denied it in this world and denied the return to God in the Hereafter, as well as for others who affirmed it. It watches and lies in wait for whoever passes by. Al-Ḥasan used to say when reciting this verse: ‘There is a guard at the gate: whoever comes with a pass gets through, and whoever comes without a pass is detained.’ Al-Ḥasan said no one enters Paradise without passing over the Fire. Qatādah said one must cross the Fire to reach Paradise. Sufyān said three bridges lie over it.

His saying, ‘a destination for the transgressors’: Hell is a lodging and place of return for those who transgressed God’s limits in this world, arrogantly defying their Lord; it is their final dwelling. Qatādah said it is a dwelling and refuge. Sufyān said it is a place of return and a dwelling.

His saying, ‘where they will remain for ages’: those who transgressed in this world will remain in Hell for ages. Readers differed over lābithīn: most Medinan and Basran readers and some Kufans read it with an alif; most Kufans read labithīn without one. The alif reading is more eloquent and more grammatical, since Arabs rarely use an adjective on the pattern faʿil to govern an object, as in ‘a stingy man with his wealth,’ ‘difficult for us,’ or ‘hostile to us.’ This pattern is normally used for praise or blame and does not govern another word. When they want it to govern a noun, they use the active participle: bākil, ‘stingy with his wealth,’ or ṭāmiʿ, ‘covetous of what we have.’ Thus lābithīn is more grammatically sound and eloquent. Al-Ṭabarī does not reject labithīn, since Arabs sometimes do use adjectives of praise and blame with nouns; Labīd’s verse gives an example, using ʿamil to govern ʿiṣādah, although ʿāmil would be more eloquent.

Another poem says, ‘With an axe, striking the heads of palm fronds.’ The same construction appears in a verse by ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās. Aḥqāb is the plural of ḥuqb; ḥuqb is the plural of ḥuqbah, as a poet says, ‘We lived like two companions of Judhaymah for an age, until it was said we would never part.’ Some take aḥqāb as the plural of ḥuqūb; the singular occurs in ‘or continue for an age’ (Q 18:60).
The interpreters differed over how long an age is.
Some said three hundred years. It is reported that an age is three hundred years, each year 360 days, each day a thousand years.

Others said an age is eighty years. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib asked Hilāl al-Hajarī what the revealed Book says about an age; he replied: eighty years, each year twelve months, each month thirty days, each day a thousand years. Abū Hurayrah gave the same number, saying each year is 360 days. Ibn ʿAbbās said it is eighty years. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also said eighty years, with a year of 360 days and a day equal to a year or a thousand years; the transmitter is uncertain which. Qatādah said it has no end: whenever one age passes, another follows; it is also reported as eighty years. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said only God knows the number of ages, but one age is eighty years, each year 360 days and each day a thousand years.

Others said one age is seventy thousand years. Al-Ḥasan said the ages have no count except that they last forever in the Fire, though it is reported that a single age is seventy thousand years, each day of those seventy thousand years equaling a thousand years of your reckoning. Another report from al-Ḥasan says no one knows what the ages are, but one age is seventy thousand years, each day like a thousand years. It is also related from Khālid ibn Maʿdān that this verse concerns members of the Muslim community. He said ‘remaining there for ages’ and ‘except as your Lord wills’ (Q 11:108) refer to monotheists among the people of the qiblah. Asked how he understands this report, al-Ṭabarī says Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas gave the sounder view: these ages have no end or termination. The disbelievers are not punished only for a limited number of ages; rather, the ages may refer to the particular kind of punishment just described—tasting neither coolness nor drink except scalding water and pus.

When those ages end, other kinds of punishment may follow, as God says: ‘This is so; and for the transgressors is an evil place of return—Hell, where they will burn; what a wretched resting place! This is so; let them taste scalding water and pus, and other kinds of similar punishment’ (Q 38:55–58). This is the interpretation that best fits the verse. A report from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān says the verse was abrogated by ‘We will increase you in nothing but punishment’ (Q 78:30). Al-Ṭabarī says this is meaningless: ‘remaining there for ages’ is a report, and reports are not abrogated; abrogation applies to commands and prohibitions. His saying, ‘They will taste neither coolness nor drink’: they will taste no coolness that relieves the heat of the blaze, except pus, and no drink that quenches their intense thirst except scalding water. Some Arabists claimed that ‘coolness’ here means sleep, so the verse would mean they taste neither sleep nor drink.

They cited a poem by al-Kindī in which coldness means drowsiness. Even if sleep cools the burning thirst and is called ‘coolness’ for that reason, it is not the word’s familiar meaning. God’s Book should be interpreted according to the most common Arabic usage.

x: The interpreters said similarly. Al-Rabīʿ explained the exception as: scalding water is excepted from drink, and pus from coolness. His saying, ‘except scalding water and pus’: they will taste neither coolness nor drink, except water heated until its heat is extreme, like molten metal, scorching faces; and they will have no coolness except pus.

The interpreters differed over the meaning of ghassāq. Some said it is what flows from the pus of Hell’s inhabitants. ʿAṭiyyah ibn Saʿd said it is what flows from their skins. ʿIkrimah said it is the pus and blood that flow from their eyes.

Ibrāhīm and Abū Razīn said ghassāq is the washings of the people of the Fire; another wording says what flows from their pus. Qatādah said it is what flows between their skin and flesh. Sufyān reported that it is what flows from their tears; Ibrāhīm said it is the cold fluid that drains from their pus, while another report from Sufyān identifies it as tears. Ibrāhīm and Abū Razīn called ghassāq the washings of the people of Hell; one wording says what drains from their pus. Qatādah said it is what flows between their skin and flesh. Sufyān reported that it may be what flows from their tears. Ibrāhīm said it is what drains from their pus because of the cold; another report identifies it as tears. Ibn Zayd said the scalding water is the tears of their eyes in the Fire, collected in trenches and then given to them to drink. Ghassāq is the pus that flows from their skins as the Fire melts them, collected in pools and given to them.
Ibrāhīm said it is what is cut away from their skins and what flows from their stench.

Others said ghassāq is bitter cold. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as zamharīr. Mujāhid said it is a cold so intense they cannot taste it. Mujāhid repeatedly explained ghassāq as cold so intense it cannot be endured. Al-Rabīʿ and Abū al-ʿĀliyah said it is zamharīr.

Others said it is foul-smelling; in the Tukhārī dialect, ghassāq means something foul. Al-Ṭabarī says ghassāq is an intensive form from the expression ‘his eye flowed’ when tears run and ‘the wound flowed’ when pus drains. The word is also used of the night when it covers things (Q 113:3), referring to its rushing over them like flowing water. Since ghassāq is something that flows, what God promises these people to taste as a drink in the Hereafter is a flowing fluid of zamharīr in Hell, combining intense cold and foulness. The Prophet said: ‘If a bucketful of ghassāq were poured into this world, it would make the people of the world stink.’ ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr said ghassāq is thick pus: if a drop were poured in the West, the people of the East would stink, and if poured in the East, the people of the West would stink.
Someone might ask how zamharīr, which is extreme cold, can be a flowing liquid.
that the unbearable cold is a quality of the fluid flowing from the people’s bodies, between pus and suppuration.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘A fitting recompense (26). They did not expect an accounting (27), and they utterly denied Our signs (28). We have recorded everything in a book (29). So taste the punishment; We will increase you in nothing but punishment (30).’ God says this punishment inflicted upon the disbelievers in the Hereafter is a recompense for their vile deeds and words in this world. It is the verbal noun from the expression ‘this punishment matched this deed.’

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as matching their deeds. Qatādah said the recompense matched the people’s evil deeds. Al-Rabīʿ said it was according to their deeds; in another report he called it a reward matching their deeds. Ibn Zayd said they did evil and were repaid with evil, and did good and were repaid with good, citing ‘Then the end of those who did evil was evil’ (Q 30:10). Qatādah likewise said the recompense matched the people’s deeds. Mujāhid said the recompense matches the deed.

His saying, ‘They did not expect an accounting’: these disbelievers did not fear that God would call them to account in the Hereafter for His blessings and kindness toward them and their poor gratitude for them. Mujāhid said they did not care and did not affirm the unseen. Qatādah explained it as not fearing an accounting. Ibn Zayd said they did not believe in resurrection or accounting: how could someone expect an accounting if he is not certain he will live again or be resurrected? He recited passages in which earlier peoples denied being brought back to life and called the claim that a man would inform them of resurrection a lie or madness (Q 23:81–83; 34:7–8). They asked about the man: ‘Has he fabricated a lie against God, or is he possessed?’—that is, is he mad to tell us this?

His saying, ‘They utterly denied Our signs’: these disbelievers denied Our proofs and evidences. The form kidhdhāban is used instead of takdhīban to match the verb. A Basran grammarian said the form faʿʿala has four consonants, and the verbal noun was fashioned after the pattern of afʿala / ifʿālan; on that analogy one can say qātala / qittālan. He said this is Arabic usage. A Kufan grammarian said it is eloquent Yemeni usage: they say kadhdhabtu bihi kidhdhāban and kharraqtu al-qamīṣ khirāqan, forming verbal nouns on fiʿʿāl from verbs on faʿʿala. He quoted an Arab who asked him whether he preferred shaving or tailoring, and a verse by a man of Banū Kilāb. Readers agreed on doubling the dhāl here. Al-Kisāʾī alone lightens it in the later verse ‘nor any denial.’ He treats the later word as coming from ‘I exchanged lies with him’ or ‘mutual denial.’ He reads this occurrence with doubling because …

His saying, ‘We have recorded everything in a book’: God says We have counted and written everything, recording its number, amount, and measure. Nothing escapes Our knowledge. ‘In a book’ is accusative because ‘We recorded it’ has the sense ‘We established and wrote it down’; it is as if the verse said, ‘We wrote everything down in a book.’

His saying, ‘So taste the punishment; We will increase you in nothing but punishment’: these disbelievers in Hell will be told, after drinking scalding water and ghassāq, ‘Taste the punishment of God that you denied in this world. We will increase you in punishment upon the punishment you already suffer, without reducing it or giving you relief.’ ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr said no verse was more severe for the people of the Fire than this one: they are continually increased in punishment. Qatādah transmitted the same statement.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘For the God-fearing there is triumph (31): gardens and grapevines (32), youthful companions of equal age (33), and a brimming cup (34). They will hear no idle talk or falsehood there (35).’ God says the God-fearing will have a deliverance from the Fire to Paradise, an escape from it, and attainment of what they sought. Mujāhid said they triumph by escaping the Fire. Qatādah said, indeed, it is triumph from the Fire to Paradise, from God’s punishment to His mercy. Ibn ʿAbbās said it is a place of recreation.

His saying, ‘gardens’: gardens explain and clarify the triumph. It is valid to use them to explain it because mafāz can mean attainment of what one seeks. The sense is that the God-fearing attain what they seek: gardens and grapevines. Ḥadāʾiq is the plural of ḥadīqah, orchards of palms, grapes, or other trees enclosed by walls. They are called ḥadīqah because the walls surround and enclose them; without surrounding walls, they are not called a ḥadīqah.
His saying, ‘and grapevines’: vines bearing grapes are meant; mention of the grapes suffices without explicitly mentioning the vines.
His saying, ‘youthful companions of equal age’: young women whose breasts have risen and who are of one age. Ibn ʿAbbās explained kawāʿib as young women who have reached maturity.

His saying, ‘of equal age’ means alike in age. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are women of equal age. Qatādah explained kawāʿib as young women whose breasts have risen, and atrāb as being of one age. He said they are women in Paradise, all of the same age. Ibn Jurayj said kawāʿib are young women whose breasts have risen. Ibn Zayd said they are women who have matured, and ‘of equal age’ means peers. Mujāhid said they are peers.

His saying, ‘and a brimming cup’: a cup filled to the top, repeatedly passed among those drinking, in abundance and fullness. The word derives from dahq, forceful and repeated pressing upon someone. A cup described as dihāq likewise comes around to drinkers repeatedly, in abundance and full measure.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās once asked his servant to bring him a dihāq; when the servant brought a full cup, he said, ‘That is dihāq.’ Ibn ʿAbbās explained dihāq as full. Ibn Zayd transmitted from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as successive, one following another; Ibn Wahb said it means one after the other. Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās says it is full. Abū Hurayrah used the word damādim. Al-Ḥasan said full; another report from him says a full cup. Mujāhid said the cup is full. Qatādah called it filled to the brim; in another report he described it as full and overflowing. Ibn Zayd said it is filled.
Others said dihāq means clear. ʿIkrimah explained it as clear.

Others said the cup comes successively, one after another. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explained it as coming in succession. Mujāhid said the same. ʿIkrimah, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās, said it is full and successive. Mujāhid likewise said it follows one cup after another.

His saying, ‘They will hear no idle talk or falsehood there’: in Paradise they will hear no idle speech, meaning vain words, and no mutual denial; none of them will call another a liar. The readers of the regions doubled the dhāl, as explained earlier in ‘they utterly denied Our signs,’ except al-Kisāʾī, who lightened it for the reason already given. Al-Ṭabarī prefers the doubled reading and does not consider the light reading permissible here, since the authoritative readers agree against it. The light form comes from ‘I exchanged lies with him’ and ‘mutual denial.’ Al-Aʿshā said: ‘I told her the truth and lied to her … a person’s lying may benefit him.’
The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah explained it as idle and sinful speech. Ibn Zayd said there is neither idle talk nor falsehood in Paradise.

x: The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘A recompense from your Lord, a gift in due measure (36), the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, the Most Compassionate, from whom they will have no power to speak (37), on the Day the Spirit and the angels stand in rows; none will speak except one whom the Most Compassionate permits and who speaks rightly (38).’ God says that He gave the God-fearing what these verses describe as a reward from their Lord for their obedience to Him in this world.

His saying, ‘a gift’: God graciously bestowed this recompense upon them. That is because … … He rewarded a single good deed tenfold in some cases and seven hundredfold in others. This increase, though a recompense, is a gift from God.
His saying, ‘in due measure’: their deeds are accounted for by God.

The interpreters said similarly. Mujāhid said it is a gift from Him, proportionate to what they did. Qatādah said it is a great gift: for a small amount of good work He gives them a magnificent, everlasting reward. He also explained it as a plentiful gift. Ibn Zayd recited the description of Paradise up to ‘a gift in due measure’ and said that this is recompense for their deeds and a gift from God: they did one deed for Him, and He rewarded it tenfold. Ibn Zayd cited ‘Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like’ (Q 6:160) and ‘The likeness of those who spend their wealth in God’s way is that of a grain that grows seven ears, each ear containing a hundred grains; God multiplies for whomever He wills’ (Q 2:261). God increases for whomever He wills. All this is a gift, not work they did to earn it: they performed ten good deeds and He gave them a hundred, or performed a hundred and He gave them a thousand. This is all a gift. He then counts it as though they had performed that amount of work, and rewards them accordingly.

His saying, ‘the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything between them, the Most Compassionate’: it is a recompense from your Lord, the Lord of the seven heavens, the earth, and all creatures between them. Readers differed: most Medinan readers read ‘Lord’ and ‘Most Compassionate’ in the nominative; some Basrans and Kufans read both in the genitive; some Meccans and most Kufans read ‘Lord’ in the genitive and ‘Most Compassionate’ in the nominative. All these readings have a valid grammatical basis. Whichever a reader uses is correct, though the genitive ‘Lord’ is preferable because it is close to ‘from your Lord,’ while the nominative ‘Most Compassionate’ is preferable because it is farther away.

evidence.text: Readers differed: most Medinan readers read ‘Lord’ and ‘Most Compassionate’ in the nominative; some Basrans and Kufans read both in the genitive; some Meccans and most Kufans read ‘Lord’ in the genitive and ‘Most Compassionate’ in the nominative.

x: His saying, ‘the Most Compassionate, from whom they will have no power to speak’: God says … … the Most Compassionate; none of His creatures will be able to address Him on the Day of Resurrection except one whom He permits and who speaks rightly. Mujāhid and Qatādah explained ‘they will have no power to speak’ as meaning they cannot speak. Ibn Zayd said they cannot address God; an interlocutor is one who argues with another.
His saying, ‘on the Day the Spirit stands’: scholars differed about the Spirit here.

Some said it is an angel of enormous creation. Ibn Masʿūd said it is an angel in the fourth heaven, greater than the heavens, mountains, and angels; each day he glorifies God twelve thousand times, and from every glorification God creates an angel. On the Day of Resurrection he comes alone in a row. Ibn ʿAbbās said it is the greatest of the angels in creation.
Others said it is Gabriel. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Shaʿbī said the Spirit is Gabriel.

Others said it is a creature of God in the form of human beings. Mujāhid said the Spirit is a creature in human form that eats and drinks. He also described them as creatures with hands, feet, and perhaps heads, who eat food but are not angels. Abū Ṣāliḥ said they resemble people but are not people. Mujāhid also said the Spirit is a creature like Adam. Al-Aʿmash said the Spirit is a creature of God, many times more numerous than the angels, with hands and feet. Abū Ṣāliḥ said the Spirit is a creature like human beings, but not human.
Others said they are the children of Adam. Qatādah and al-Ḥasan said the Spirit is the children of Adam. Qatādah added that Ibn ʿAbbās kept this interpretation private.

Others said the Spirit means the souls of the children of Adam. Ibn ʿAbbās explained that it is when people’s souls stand with the angels between the two trumpet blasts, before the souls are returned to their bodies.

Others said the Spirit is the Qur’an. Ibn Zayd said his father used to say that it is the Qur’an, citing ‘Thus We revealed to you a spirit by Our command; you did not know what the Book or faith was’ (Q 42:52). The correct approach, al-Ṭabarī says, is to state that God reports His creatures will have no power to address Him when the Spirit stands, and that the Spirit is one of His creatures. It could be any of the things listed; God knows which one is intended. No report that must be accepted identifies one meaning to the exclusion of the rest, and not knowing which it is causes no harm. It is also said that two rows will stand. Al-Shaʿbī said they are two rows belonging to the Lord of the worlds: one row of the Spirit and one of angels.

His saying, ‘none will speak except one whom the Most Compassionate permits’: it is said they will be permitted to speak when the people of the Fire are led to the Fire and the people of Paradise to Paradise. ʿIkrimah related that angels will ask about groups being led away; they will be told the people of the Fire go there because of what their hands earned and that God did not wrong them. When people of Paradise pass, the angels will ask where they are going and be told that they enter Paradise through God’s mercy. Then they will be permitted to speak.

Others said the permission is for one who affirmed God’s oneness in this world and ‘spoke rightly’ by declaring His unity. Ibn ʿAbbās said it means the Lord permits the testimony that there is no god but God, the utmost truth. Mujāhid said the person spoke the truth in this world and acted upon it. Abū Ṣāliḥ and ʿIkrimah explained ‘spoke rightly’ as saying ‘There is no god but God.’ Al-Ṭabarī says the correct view is simply what God reports: on the Day the Spirit and angels stand in rows, none will speak except one whom the Most Compassionate permits and who speaks rightly. Since God and His Messenger have not specified a particular kind of truthful speech, and the wording can encompass all of them, it should be left general.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘That is the True Day. Whoever wishes may take a way back to his Lord (39). We have warned you of an imminent punishment: the Day a person will see what his hands have sent ahead, and the disbeliever will say, “If only I were dust!” (40)’ God says ‘that Day’ means the Day of Resurrection, when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows. ‘The True’ means that it will certainly occur, without doubt.

His saying, ‘Whoever wishes may take a way back to his Lord’: whoever among God’s servants wishes may take … … a way back to his Lord by affirming this true Day, preparing for it, and doing what will save him from its terrors. Maʾāb means a place of return, on the pattern mafʿil, from the expression ‘so-and-so returned from his journey.’ ʿUbayd said: ‘Everyone who is away returns, but one absent through death does not return.’ Qatādah said they take a way back to God through obedience and what brings them near to Him. Sufyān said it means a path, a place of return, and a dwelling.

His saying, ‘We have warned you of an imminent punishment’: people, We have warned you of a punishment that has drawn near. That is the Day when the believer sees what his hands sent ahead of good deeds earned in this world, or evil deeds he committed. He hopes for God’s reward for his good deeds and fears His punishment for his bad ones.
The interpreters said similarly. Al-Ḥasan said the person is the believer, who is wary of small sins and fears major ones. Another report from him likewise says the person is the believer.

His saying, ‘and the disbeliever will say, “If only I were dust!”’: on that Day the disbeliever will wish he were dust, because of the punishment God has prepared for those who disbelieved in Him, like the beasts that are turned to dust.

The interpreters said similarly. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr said the earth will be spread out like a hide, and beasts, livestock, and wild animals will be gathered. Judgment will be exacted among them: a hornless sheep will receive justice against a horned sheep that butted it. When judgment among the animals is finished, they will be told, ‘Become dust.’ At that point the disbeliever will say, ‘If only I were dust!’ Abū Hurayrah said God will gather all creatures—every beast, bird, and human—and tell the beasts and birds to become dust; then the disbeliever will say, ‘If only I were dust!’ The Prophet said God will judge among jinn, humans, and beasts, giving the hornless animal its due from the horned one until no claim remains between them. Then God will say, ‘Become dust,’ and the disbeliever will say, ‘If only I were dust!’ Qatādah described him as ruined, negligent, and helpless: what could keep him from saying it after his deeds’ shameful faults have been exposed and he stands before the Most Compassionate, who is angry with him?

He will wish for death, though nothing in this world was more hateful to him than death. Abū al-Zinād said that when judgment among people is complete and the people of Hell are ordered to the Fire, the believing jinn and all nations other than the children of Adam will be told, ‘Return to dust.’ When the disbelievers see them turned to dust, the disbeliever will say, ‘If only I were dust!’ Sufyān likewise said that when beasts are told to become dust, the disbeliever will say it. This is the end of the commentary on Sūrat ʿAmma Yatasāʾalūn.

notes.en: Al-misḥal is a male wild ass, and saḥīl is its call. ʿIḍādat samḥaj is one of its flanks; a samḥaj is a long-backed female wild ass. Sarāt means the upper back; nadab means scratches and marks, plural of nadbah; kulūm are wounds from bites. See the commentary on Labīd’s Dīwān, p. 125.
notes.ar: المسحل: الفحل من الحُمُر، وسحيله: صوته. وعضادة سمحج: أحد شقيها. والسمحج: الأتان الطويلة الظهر. وسراتها: أعلى ظهرها والندب: خدوش وآثار، جمع نَدَبة. والكلوم: جراحات من عضه إياها. شرح ديوان البيد ص 125.

notes.en: This is the second hemistich of a verse in Maʿānī al-Qurʾān of al-Farrāʾ 3/228 and in Lisān al-ʿArab, root Z-ʿ-B, without attribution. The first hemistich in Lisān al-ʿArab is: ‘From the surging mass, he has not struck an enemy with his sword.’

notes.en: Al-karānif is plural of karnāf/karnāfah, the thick base of a palm frond at the trunk. See Lisān al-ʿArab, root K-R-N-F.
notes.ar: الكرانف: جمع الكرناف والكرنافة، بضم الكاف وكسرها وهى أصل السعفة الغليظة في جذع النخلة. ينظر اللسان (كرنف).
